correctness.rationale: Reflection of all three coordinates preserves both the flow and H, so consider x>0. The exact identities for w=z+x^q y are xw=h+y²/2 and w'=−x^(q−1)y². Hence 0<w≤w(0) and x≥h/w(0), excluding the interface. When y≤0 its derivative is positive; when y≥0 it satisfies y'≤w(0)−(h/w(0))^q y. These bounds on y, hence on x and z over finite intervals, give forward continuation. If y never becomes positive, x stays bounded above and y'≥h/sup(x)>0, a contradiction; upward crossing at y=0 prevents a return to negative y. Bounded increasing x would imply y'≥h/sup(x)−sup(x)^q y and thus positive limiting lower velocity, again impossible. With x→infinity, any fixed positive velocity level is eventually crossed downward because y'≤w(0)−x^q y, so y→0. On y=b=(1±epsilon)h x^(−q−1), the derivative of y−b is ∓epsilon h/x+(q+3/2)b²/x, giving inward signs at large x. Remaining forever above the upper barrier forces y'≤−epsilon h/(2x) at late times, and remaining below the lower forces y'≥epsilon h/x. Bounded y gives x=O(1+t), so neither is possible by the divergent integral of 1/x. The eventual inward trap yields x^(q+1)y→h, and integrating (x^(q+2))' proves the original-time position limit. Reflection gives the sign in the velocity limit. This checks every positive level including q=1 on the open half-lines, not the zero level, interface dynamics or backward time.
